Taking waste management seriously. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Dhaka’s waste management system is failing to keep pace with its growing needs, and our roads and footpaths turning into dumping grounds is yet another indication of just that.
Overflowing bins, exposed garbage, and poorly located secondary transfer stations are not merely an eyesore; they obstruct pedestrians, worsen traffic congestion, and expose residents to foul odours, wastewater, and serious environmental and public-health risks.
The scale of the challenge makes a more systematic approach imperative.
The two city corporations reportedly collect around 6,500 tons of waste every day, and operate 118 temporary secondary transfer stations, in addition to the permanent landfill sites at Aminbazar and Matuail.
Yet the continued presence of waste on public roads demonstrates that collection alone cannot constitute effective waste management.
The authorities must first reconsider the placement and design of waste transfer stations: Facilities located beside busy roads, schools, hospitals, shops, and residential areas inevitably create public-health and mobility problems.
Properly designed, enclosed, and strategically located stations, equipped with adequate capacity and drainage, should therefore replace makeshift dumping points.
Collection schedules must also become more reliable. Waste should not be allowed to accumulate until bins overflow onto public spaces.
Greater investment in covered vehicles, efficient transportation, and modern treatment and disposal facilities is necessary, alongside stricter monitoring of contractors and city corporation workers.
At the same time, waste segregation at source should become a central component of the city’s long-term strategy. Separating organic, recyclable, and hazardous waste would make recycling and composting more viable while reducing pressure on landfills.
Public awareness campaigns must accompany this, because no municipal system can succeed if citizens continue to dump waste indiscriminately.
Most importantly, responsibility must be clearly assigned and enforced effectively. Dhaka’s residents deserve clean, accessible footpaths and roads, not garbage-filled public spaces.
Waste management must be treated as essential urban infrastructure, because the residents deserve a Dhaka with clean, garbage-free public spaces.

item.title: Can we fix bad loans?. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Bangladesh Bank’s decision to adopt an 18-month action plan to tackle the country’s alarming non-performing loan (NPL) problem is both necessary and long overdue.
With roughly 36% of the banking sector’s total loans reportedly classified as non-performing, the scale of the crisis poses a serious threat -- not only to banks but to the wider economy.
The immediate priority must be to ensure that the plan translates into measurable recovery rather than becoming another policy exercise. The proposed measures, including stronger supervision, faster recovery mechanisms, legal reforms, and opportunities for settlement, can help reduce the burden of bad loans.
However, flexibility must not become an avenue for habitual defaulters to escape accountability. Any settlement or restructuring facility should therefore be transparent, conditional, and strictly targeted at genuinely viable businesses facing temporary difficulties.
At the same time, Bangladesh must address the reasons why NPLs have accumulated so dramatically. Weak due diligence, politically-influenced lending, inadequate risk assessment, and poor corporate governance have allowed borrowers to obtain credit without sufficient regard for repayment capacity.
Effective NPL management consequently requires stronger credit appraisal, independent boards, improved internal controls, and rigorous monitoring of large exposures.
Legal reform is just as crucial; lengthy recovery proceedings have historically weakened banks’ ability to reclaim funds, while repeated rescheduling can encourage strategic default.
A more efficient system for resolving distressed assets would thus allow banks to recover capital, and redirect it towards productive investment.
Most importantly, the burden of cleaning up the banking sector cannot fall on taxpayers or honest borrowers indefinitely. Banks must strengthen provisioning and capital positions, while regulators must enforce prudential standards consistently.
The current NPL crisis is ultimately a crisis of governance and accountability. Bangladesh Bank’s roadmap is an encouraging starting point, but its success will depend on sustained enforcement, institutional independence and a firm refusal to repeat the practices that created the problem in the first place.

Turkey backs Saudi-led maritime defence coalition in Red Sea. [ middleeasteye ]
item.description:
Turkey backs Saudi-led maritime defence coalition in Red Sea

Submitted by Ragip Soylu on Thu, 08/13/2026 - 10:37
The move would help deepen the trilateral defence pact between Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan
Turkish Navy helicopters and ships on military exercises in the Mediterranean Sea near Antalya on 9 April (AFP/Adem Altan)
Off

Turkey confirmed on Thursday for the first time that it had joined efforts to establish a multinational maritime defence coalition aimed at ensuring freedom of navigation in the Red Sea.

The announcement signals increased cooperation between Saudi Arabia and Ankara after the signing of a trilateral pact between the states and Pakistan in Mecca last week.

“At the invitation of Saudi Arabia, a technical meeting was held in Riyadh on 28 July to ensure freedom of navigation through the Bab al-Mandab Strait, followed by a meeting of the chiefs of general staff on 30 July 2026,” the Turkish Ministry of National Defence said in a statement.

The ministry added that Turkey was participating in another coordination meeting on the establishment of the maritime defence coalition in Jeddah on Thursday.

“Work continues with the Saudi Arabian authorities to reduce tensions in the Gulf region and ensure the uninterrupted flow of international trade,” the statement said.

Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signed a defence pact last week committing the three countries to each other’s security, including collective security obligations.

Several Ankara-based sources who spoke to Middle East Eye said they believed the Red Sea coalition would be the first area in which the alliance between Turkey and Saudi Arabia would deepen.

Saudi Arabia announced last month that it had established a 13-country maritime alliance to safeguard security in the Red Sea.

The move followed the Houthis’ declaration on 20 July that they had imposed a maritime blockade on the kingdom, disrupting oil shipments diverted to the Red Sea following the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

The alliance reportedly includes Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Pakistan, Bahrain, Bangladesh, Comoros, Djibouti, Egypt, Jordan, Kuwait, Qatar,  Somalia and Yemen.

It will be headquartered in Riyadh.

item.title: Rising heat in Asia: The toll it takes on your organs. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Thirty-year-old Vaishnavi Sharma works at an advertising agency in Gurugram and travels nearly 90 kilometres daily to reach her office from her home in Ghaziabad, Uttar Pradesh, India. She says travelling doesn’t drain her as much as the heat does.
Detailing a recent incident, Sharma tells Asian Dispatch : “It was around 8:30 in the night, I left the office and reached the [Sikanderpur] metro station. By the time I reached, I felt drained because of the heat. I could not take the stairs or elevator. I had to sit there for five minutes and ask somebody to get me a bottle of water.”
Sharma says she has been travelling long distances for work for years but now the sun feels harsher and unbearable. “You can't sit without covering your face. Earlier, I was able to easily sit in an auto for a longer duration but now even if the temperature is comparatively lower, I feel I can't step out.”
Sharma also spoke about developing skin allergies, experiencing hair loss, and pigmentation around her face, hands, and feet due to the heat.
A 23-year-old student from Dhaka, Bangladesh, Fariha Tasnim, studies at the University of Asia Pacific (UAP). She says, “I have developed rashes on my body, I am unable to sleep at night because of the heat. My body feels dehydrated, and in some cases, when the heat becomes extremely intense, blister-like spots appear.”
Picture1
Fariha Tasnim, a 23-year-old student studying at University of Asia Pacific (UAP) in Dhaka in Bangladesh.
Tasnim spends nearly six hours on an average in the heat every day. She travels to her university to attend classes and then to the homes of the students she teaches. She mentions that going outside in the heat is unavoidable because of college and work.
Sharma and Tasnim’s experience highlight the impact heat has on people’s health. While these are anecdotes, studies also note that heat increases health risks such as heat strokes and makes non-communicable diseases such as diabetes and hypertension worse.
However, these cases are not limited to India or Bangladesh, the pattern is consistent across Asia.
According to the World Meteorological Organization (WMO), Asia has warmed up faster than the global average in the recent decades.
It also accounted for 45% of the global heat-related deaths between 2000-2019.
So, why is Asia warming up so fast?
Gautam Menon, a professor of physics and biology at Ashoka University, said that the greater rise in temperature is because of the region’s larger landmass.
“The impacts of climate change are not uniform across the globe, even as there is a general increase in global temperatures. The large continental landmass of Asia means that higher temperatures can be sustained over longer periods, and Asia has warmed significantly faster than the rest of the world. The experience of heat depends on several local factors, among them [is] built urban environments, as cities in Asia increasingly urbanize”, Menon says.
Menon also explained how this heat puts a burden on the human body. “Extreme heat places increased demands on the body, calling on greater resources. Unless one is well hydrated, increased demands are placed on the kidneys, among other organs, while heat stress affects every organ in both direct and indirect ways.”
The heart
“To keep the body cool, blood-vessels will start dilating, and they become warmer. So, the sweating increases. Sweating is also a part of the body’s mechanism to cool down. Whenever there is sweating, there is a loss of salt and electrolytes from the body. It can cause a decrease in the total body water as well as the electrolytes. Now, suppose somebody is healthy, all these things are manageable. But when somebody who has got heart disease or is a patient of heart failure, or has blocked arteries, or high blood-pressure, this can cause issues with the heart.” - Dr Rahul Gupta, Director and Head of Cardiology and Structural Heart Program, Gleneagles Hospitals
Dr Gupta said that the water and electrolyte imbalances can cause:
A study published in 2022 said that “a 1°C increase in temperature was positively associated with cardiovascular disease-related mortality across all considered diagnoses. The overall risk of cardiovascular disease-related mortality increased by 2.1%.”
The brain
“The bad impact on the brain - especially for the neurological side - is that these heat waves can increase certain neurological disorders because the brain as well as the nerves are very sensitive to high core temperatures. It can damage the nerves, which are present in the brain as well as the spinal nerves. It can also damage the blood-brain barrier.” - Dr Puneet Agarwal, Vice-Chairman of Neurology, Max HealthCare
Dr Agarwal said that if the core body temperature goes beyond over 40°C or 104°F, then the nerves in the body and blood-brain barrier gets affected and damaged. This can lead to swelling in the nerves and brain.
The usual symptoms are:
Multiple studies have concluded that long-term exposure to extreme high temperatures can lead to cognitive decline.
The liver
“When the core [body] temperature goes above 40°C, it causes hepatocyte [damage], meaning liver cells damage and necrosis. There could also be dehydration. Dehydration would lead to reduced blood flow. That will cause an ischemia-reperfusion injury because of the sluggish flow or reduced flow.” - Dr Chetan Kalal, Associate Director, Hepatology and Liver Transplant, Gleneagles Hospital
Dr Kalal said that the liver is among the first organs to fail in these extreme heat conditions.
A research paper published in January 2026 also highlighted that the liver is one of the earliest organs to be damaged in case of a heat-induced multiple organ dysfunction syndrome. The paper said that the liver is particularly vulnerable to temperature fluctuations. Acute liver injury (ALI) and acute liver failure (ALF) are serious complications and are direct causes of patient death.
The kidneys
“People who have pre-existing hypertension, diabetes, chronic kidney disease or at risk of developing further worsening of kidney functions. This is because of the excess volume depletion due to profuse sweating causing further kidney injury. People who do not have any previous kidney problems also are at risk of developing acute kidney injury.” - Dr S Sathiyan, Senior Consultant, Nephrology, SIMS Hospital
He said that extreme heat can also lead to:
A research paper published in March 2026 noted, “Multiple studies across diverse settings have shown increased hospital admissions for acute kidney injury on days of high ambient temperature and during heatwave.”
Who is most affected?
People who work outdoors during peak hours such as construction workers, farmers, and gig workers are the most vulnerable group to illnesses related to rising temperature. People with pre-existing medical conditions, elderly, children, and pregnant women also come under this category.
I met Yogendra Prasad, 33, who hails from Ayodhya, Uttar Pradesh, India works for a company that conducts surveys in Delhi. He travels everyday via bus to meet people and takes photographs of shops in Delhi to collect data for his company. Prasad says he faces difficulties in summers and sometimes experiences dizziness but he has to do his work.
Picture1
Yogendra Yadav, 33, carries a cloth over his head to protect himself from the heat. Photo: Shivansh Srivastava/Asian Dispatch
There are many more like Prasad.
Picture1
Pappu Yadav, 36, runs a paratha shop in Jasola Vihar, Delhi, in India. Photo: Shivansh Srivastava/Asian Dispatch
Dr Subarna Goswami, a public-health administrator based in West Bengal, argued that the construction workers, people working on the roads under the sun, and the working class are the “people who contribute the least to this global warming but are the worst victims.”
Sharma’s battle with heat and responsibilities don’t end with her work shift either. She mentioned that after completing work and reaching home, she cooks dinner for herself and her family. “I stand in the kitchen, even if there is ventilation, I have to stand in front of the gas. So again, I have to stand in heat. I don't think I am able to relax in the AC again until 11pm”, she says.
The future that lies ahead
Menon argues that given the pace of climate change, there is almost nothing that can be done over a short period of time.
"Given the pace of climate change, historical emissions, and the inertia of the climate system, there is almost nothing that governments can do that might make a difference over the short to intermediate term. Over the long term, over a century or more, an immediate reduction in emissions will have an impact, but it will again take a long time to stabilize. It should be an absolute priority to reduce carbon emissions to levels of about a century ago, through the use of renewables", Menon says.
He suggests that the governments across Asia should mitigate and adapt. Some of the long-term methods to deal with the rising temperature and climate change, at large, could be:

item.title: The quiet geometry of a balancing act. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
For weeks, speculation over Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's first foreign trip ran through Dhaka's political class with much intensity. India, Turkey, and the United Kingdom were all floated in turn, fed by nothing more than the silence of those who actually knew.
The travel date itself was disclosed only two days ahead of departure, and when the delegation was finally named, it was pointedly lean: No sprawling political entourage, only the relevant officials the visit required.
The destination was Kuala Lumpur, then Beijing, a pairing that answered the earlier guesswork with a kind of quiet deliberateness. The groundwork, it turned out, had been laid well before departure: Senior officials had made repeated visits to both capitals in the preceding months, and Bangladesh's presence at the World Economic Forum event meant that it was well planned from before.
And once underway, it turned into an argument -- the one this government has made its signature. " Shobar aage Bangladesh ," or "Bangladesh first." It is an easy phrase to print on a banner and a hard one to honour,, where slogans tend to die quiet deaths in the white space between diplomatic communiqués.
What this tour demonstrated is that the phrase was actually meant to be operative instead of just being ornamental. A foreign policy organized around the country's needs: Jobs, investment, market access, and the dignity of millions of Bangladeshis whose remittances keep the national ledger breathing.
Malaysia made plain sense as the opening stop. A major Muslim-majority Southeast Asian economy, home to a vast Bangladeshi workforce, and a gateway to the regional architecture Dhaka has long wished to enter the Asean in any format.
It also carried weight on a question closer to home: With more than a million Rohingya still sheltered in Cox's Bazar and no credible path to repatriation in sight, Malaysia's standing within the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) and its voice among Asean member states make its support worth courting.
The prime minister raised both threads with his counterpart, Anwar Ibrahim -- pressing for a labour corridor that manages demand transparently, defines requirements clearly, and safeguards the welfare of Bangladeshi workers rather than leaving them exposed to predatory recruitment.
Beyond labour, the two governments agreed to work towards a free trade agreement by 2027, and Malaysia lent its support to Bangladesh's aspiration to join the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership and to secure Asean Sectoral Dialogue Partner status.
Then came China, and the elevation of the register that China always demands. The prime minister was received by the three powerful figures in the Chinese state - President Xi Jinping, Premier Li Qiang, and the chairman of the National People's Congress in Beijing.
Beijing voiced support for Dhaka's ambitions toward Brics and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, agreed a strategic dialogue between the two foreign ministers, and discussed within its capacity about the comprehensive management of the Teesta. Ahead of the visit, the government cleared the roughly Tk 4,189 crore infrastructure plan for the Chinese Economic and Industrial Zone in Anwara. The runway on which a hoped-for half a billion dollars of investment and a hundred thousand jobs are meant, in time, to land.
Dhaka did not conclude a free trade agreement with Beijing. It signed memoranda, framed the Teesta engagement as a matter of feasibility rather than strategic embrace, and ensured the communiqué stated plainly that the cooperation is directed at no third party. That restraint is not timid.
Four months earlier, Bangladesh signed an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade with the United States , which is a significant agenda. It lowered the reciprocal tariff on Bangladeshi exports and opened the prospect of zero-tariff treatment for garments made with American cotton, no small thing for the industry that is the spine of the economy.
That agreement also set boundaries: It provided that a preferential economic pact with a country Washington designates as "non-market" could place the tariff relief at risk. The balancing act, then, is not a rhetorical flourish about being friends with everyone. It is a real constraint, and the Beijing visit was calibrated precisely not to unsettle others whilst following what is best for the country.
It honoured the commitment to Washington and the welcome in Beijing, and it has continued to engage New Delhi in parallel, the prime minister having already received an invitation to visit.
A word of realism is owed, because analysis is not flattery. A communiqué is only a promissory note, not a delivered project, and Bangladesh's historic difficulty has never been signing agreements but absorbing them.
Vietnam sustains close ties with Washington and attracts vast Chinese investment at once, because it has built the institutional capacity to metabolize both. Our task is the same: To move faster, to lighten the bureaucratic weight that sits on ambition, and to ensure that a memorandum signed with fanfare becomes a factory that employs.
The Anwara zone has been long in the waiting; the labour corridor remains, for now, a principle rather than a passage. The gains of this tour are real, but they are options purchased and an option only has value when it is exercised.
So the verdict should be confident and clear-eyed at once. In a single tour, Tarique Rahman showed that Bangladesh can compose a sophisticated foreign policy sentence: Independent in its choices, plural in its partnerships, disciplined within real constraints, and answerable first to its own people's needs.
The next chapter is delivery. For “ Shobar aage Bangladesh” to mean everything its authors intend, the order must now hold in implementation as surely as it has held in diplomacy because a country that learns to put itself first abroad must also learn to deliver for itself at home.
Ashfaq Zaman is the founder of Dhaka Forum and a strategic international affairs expert.

item.title: When the waters recede, inequality remains. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The floodwater has disappeared from Satkania and Banshkhali. Roads are reopening, markets are slowly filling with customers again, and children are beginning to return to school. To many, the crisis is over.
But for the families I met during a recent visit to these flood-hit communities, the real struggle has only just begun.
Climate disasters do not affect everyone equally. They expose the inequalities that already exist -- between women and men, girls and boys, rich and poor, those with disabilities and those without, and between households with support and those left to cope alone.
The July flash floods in Chittagong were not just an environmental disaster; they were a stark reminder that vulnerability is deeply shaped by gender and intersecting social realities. Homes collapsed, crops were destroyed, roads disappeared under water, and access to healthcare, education, and safe drinking water was severely disrupted. Yet behind these statistics are stories that reveal what disaster truly looks like.
In Ilsha village of Banshkhali, I met Shifa, a 14-year-old girl who dreams of becoming an Army officer. When the flood struck, her family fled with nothing. Returning home, they found their mud house damaged and her schoolbooks buried beneath thick mud.
Her father is undergoing cancer treatment and fears he can no longer afford to keep her in school. The flood also coincided with her menstruation, leaving her without privacy or adequate facilities to manage it safely.
For many, the flood damaged a house. For Shifa, it threatened a future.
Climate disasters interrupt far more than infrastructure. They interrupt education, aspirations, and the life chances of adolescent girls. Every missed examination, every destroyed textbook and every financial setback pushes girls closer to dropping out of school or being married early.
In the Nolua Union of Satkania, Sadia showed me another face of vulnerability. As the head of her household and sole caregiver of her three-year-old child with a disability, she faced the flood entirely alone.
She carried household belongings to safety while caring for her child, managed without menstrual hygiene products by tearing pieces from an old saree, and developed painful skin infections after prolonged exposure to contaminated floodwater. Her husband works abroad but is seriously ill and unable to support the family financially.
Sadia's experience cannot be explained by gender alone. It is the intersection of gender, disability, poverty, and unpaid caregiving that placed her at far greater risk than others around her.
That is the essence of intersectionality. Disasters may strike an entire community, but they do not strike everyone with equal force.
The same pattern emerged in the story of Parvin Akter, a widow raising three daughters on her own. During displacement, one of her adolescent daughters started menstruating without access to sanitary materials or a private place to change.
After returning home, soaring food prices forced impossible choices between buying food, hygiene supplies and school materials. Poverty did not simply make recovery harder; being a female-headed household multiplied those challenges.
Older women faced another layer of exclusion. Shefali Rani Das, aged 60, described being trapped inside her flooded home because she could barely move through the water.
Cooking became impossible, toilets disappeared beneath floodwater, and damaged roads isolated her community. Without nearby emergency shelters or reliable assistance, surviving the flood depended largely on family members who could help her move.
Throughout the visit, one reality surfaced repeatedly but rarely appears in official damage assessments: Disasters dramatically increase women's unpaid care work.
Women cleaned mud-filled homes, searched for water, cooked under impossible conditions, cared for sick children and elderly relatives, repaired damaged houses and tried to restore some sense of normalcy -- all while carrying the emotional burden of holding families together.
Recovery begins long before humanitarian assistance arrives, and much of that recovery rests on invisible, unpaid labour performed by women.
The women and girls I spoke with rarely asked for sympathy. They asked for dignity.
They spoke about inaccessible toilets, the absence of menstrual hygiene materials, damaged schools, skin diseases caused by contaminated water, and the anxiety of not knowing how they would rebuild their lives.
As climate change intensifies, Bangladesh will experience more frequent and severe weather extremes. Whether these hazards become humanitarian disasters depends not only on rainfall or river levels but on how prepared we are to protect those facing multiple and overlapping vulnerabilities.
An intersectional approach must move from policy language to practice. That means prioritising female-headed households, adolescent girls, older persons, persons with disabilities, pregnant and lactating women, and caregivers in disaster preparedness and recovery.
It means designing accessible shelters, ensuring dignified menstrual hygiene management, expanding cash assistance, strengthening psychosocial support, and recognising and reducing women's unpaid care work as part of resilience building.
What gave me some hope in Satkania and Banshkhali were the people. Neighbours rescued one another before formal relief arrived. Families shared food with those who had none. Girls like Shifa still spoke confidently about becoming Army officers, teachers and professionals despite everything they had lost.
They do not need pity. They need policies that see them.
When the next flood comes -- and it will -- the greatest danger will not only be the rising water. It will be our failure to recognize that vulnerability is never one-dimensional, and that building resilience begins by putting those standing in the deepest water at the centre of our response.
Rowshon Akhter Urmee is a Gender Justice & Social Inclusion Specialist, Oxfam in Bangladesh.
